analysis.one_liner: Replaces the child tax credit with a larger, refundable $1,000 credit per child.
analysis.headline: A bill to make the child tax credit refundable and worth up to $1,000 per child died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: At the time, the child tax credit was worth up to $500 per child and could only reduce taxes a family actually owed — so a family with low earnings got little or nothing. This bill would have replaced it with a $1,000-per-child credit that the government pays out even when it exceeds the family's tax bill, phasing down only for households earning above roughly $110,000 for couples. It would also adjust the credit and income thresholds for inflation each year. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with children, especially low- and middle-income working families. Because the credit would be refundable, families who owe little or no federal income tax would receive the money as a payment rather than losing it — the main difference from the credit in law at the time.

how_it_helps.text: Allows a tax credit of $1,000 per qualifying child, double the $500 credit then in law [S2] [S3].

Makes the credit refundable, meaning families who owe less tax than the credit amount would still receive the full benefit — under the existing credit, families with low tax bills got nothing [S2] [S3].
Phases the credit down by $50 for each $1,000 of income above $110,000 for couples and $75,000 for single filers, so the largest benefit goes to families below those incomes [S3].
Adjusts the credit amount and income thresholds for inflation each year after 2001, so the benefit would not shrink in real terms over time [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally, through the added cost to the Treasury of a larger refundable credit. Higher-income households above the phase-down thresholds would receive reduced or no credit compared with a version without income limits.

drawbacks.text: The credit's cost to the Treasury would be substantial, since a fully refundable $1,000-per-child credit pays out to millions of households regardless of tax owed; the bill contains no offsetting revenue and the record does not score its cost [S3].

The credit phases out for married couples at the same combined income threshold as single filers face individually ($110,000 joint vs. $75,000 single), a structure that creates a marriage penalty some critics of child-credit designs have pointed to [S3].

The bill requires a full 12-month taxable year to claim the credit, which in most cases effectively requires a full year of qualifying, though it carves out an exception when the year ends in the taxpayer's death [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver a meaningful cash benefit to families with children, with the design weighted toward low- and middle-income households through refundability and the income phase-down. Its honest cost is revenue: the bill includes no pay-for, so the full amount would add to the deficit or require future offsets. As drafted it was a straightforward benefit expansion rather than a carefully budgeted one.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in late September 2000 and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

narrative.text: Sen. Rod Grams introduced the bill on September 28, 2000 [S1] [S5].
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, the committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation [S5].
No further action was taken — no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote — before the 106th Congress ended [S1] [S5].
No senator signed on as a cosponsor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No group fought the bill; it simply died from inaction. Families with children did not receive the larger refundable credit, and the federal Treasury kept the revenue the bill would have cost. Its sponsor, who had no cosponsors and was not returned to the Senate that November, gained nothing from the outcome.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Treasury kept the revenue; families gained nothing

for.name: Sen. Rod Grams
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks, but attracted no cosponsors and no committee action.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on September 28, 2000 and took no further action on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, so no partisan pattern of support or opposition ever took shape.
